title: Writing files: atomic writes, permissions, bufio.Writer
summary: Buffer many small writes with bufio.Writer and always Flush; check the error from Close on files you wrote. To replace a file that matters, write a temp file in the same directory and rename it over the target.

examples.title: bufio.Writer, the Close error, O_APPEND and O_EXCL

annotations.note: os.Create truncates an existing file to zero bytes before you write anything. From this line on, the old content is gone, which is the problem the second example solves.

A buffered write can succeed in memory and fail when the OS finally writes it (disk full, network drive). Close is where that surfaces, so for files you write, join its error into the result instead of a bare defer f.Close().

bufio.Writer collects small writes and hands them to the file 4096 bytes at a time. The output shows the file holding exactly one full buffer while 2583 bytes still sit in memory: return without Flush and the tail of the report is silently lost.
OpenFile is the general form behind Open and Create. O_APPEND makes every write land at the current end of file, which is what log files want. The 0o644 is used only if the file is created.

O_CREATE|O_EXCL creates the file only if it doesn't exist, in one step, with no gap between checking and creating. Use it for lock files and to avoid overwriting a user's file. Test the error with errors.Is and fs.ErrExist: the message text differs between Windows and Linux.

examples.title: Temp file plus rename versus writing in place

annotations.note: The naive version: truncate, then write. If the process dies, the disk fills or the encoder fails in between, the file holds a prefix of the new content and the old content is gone.
The temp file goes in the target's directory, not os.TempDir(): a rename cannot move a file to another file system or volume, and /tmp is often a separate one (tmpfs, or a different Docker volume).
On any error after this point, close and delete the temp file. A hard crash skips this cleanup, so a stray "atomic.json.tmp-123" can still appear; a recognizable name lets a startup job remove them.

CreateTemp creates the file with mode 0o600. Without this Chmod, every save would silently tighten the target from 0o644 to 0o600. On Windows only the owner-write bit is used, as the read-only attribute.

Sync asks the OS to put the data on stable storage before the rename makes it visible under the real name. Without it, a power cut right after the rename can leave a correctly named but empty file on some file systems.
The in-place file is now invalid JSON; the atomic one still has version 1, because the failed write never got the real name.

use_cases: bufio.Writer: CSV and report exports, any loop that writes many small pieces
Temp file plus rename: config and state files, caches, generated assets, anything another process reads while you write
O_APPEND: log and audit files several writers append to
O_CREATE|O_EXCL: lock files and "don't overwrite the user's file" saves
strengths: os.WriteFile covers the small case in one call, like Python's Path.write_text or Node's fs.writeFileSync
bufio.Writer wraps any io.Writer (file, socket, gzip stream), not just files, unlike Java's separate BufferedWriter and BufferedOutputStream classes
The atomic pattern needs only CreateTemp, Sync, Close and Rename from the standard library
weaknesses: The standard library has no WriteFileAtomic; you write (and test) the helper yourself
Errors surface late: a buffered write succeeds in memory and fails at Flush or Close, so both must be checked
Permission bits are Unix concepts: on Windows only the owner-write bit does anything (it maps to the read-only attribute)

pitfalls.title: Forgetting Flush
pitfalls.detail: bufio.Writer holds up to 4096 bytes in memory. Return without Flush and the end of the file is missing, with no error anywhere.

pitfalls.title: Ignoring Close on a file you wrote
pitfalls.detail: defer f.Close() discards the error. For files you read that's fine; for files you wrote, join Close's error into the function's result.

pitfalls.title: Truncating a file that matters, then writing it
pitfalls.detail: os.WriteFile and os.Create truncate first. The os.WriteFile docs say it outright: a failure mid-operation can leave the file partially written. Write a temp file and rename it.

pitfalls.title: Temp file in os.TempDir()
pitfalls.detail: Rename across file systems fails (EXDEV on Linux, and Windows refuses to move across volumes). Create the temp file in the target's directory.

pitfalls.title: Losing the original permissions
pitfalls.detail: CreateTemp uses 0o600 and rename keeps the temp file's mode, so call f.Chmod(perm) before renaming.

quiz.q: A function writes 300 short lines through bufio.NewWriter(f) and returns without calling Flush. What ends up in the file?
options: All 300 lines: Close flushes the buffer
Only the bytes that filled whole 4096-byte buffers
quiz.why: Closing the *os.File knows nothing about the bufio.Writer wrapped around it; whatever is still buffered is lost.

quiz.q: Why must the temp file be created in the target's directory?
options: Rename can't move a file across file systems or volumes
So the file inherits the directory's permissions
quiz.why: os.TempDir() is often another file system or volume, where rename fails. Same directory means same file system.

quiz.q: You save config.json (mode 0o644) with CreateTemp plus Rename and no Chmod. What mode does it have afterwards on Linux?
quiz.why: Rename replaces the directory entry with the temp file, mode included. CreateTemp creates files with 0o600 before umask.

further_reading.title: package os: WriteFile, CreateTemp, Rename, OpenFile

body:
## Concept

Three layers, from simple to safe:

- `os.WriteFile(name, data, perm)` writes a whole `[]byte` in one call. It creates or
  **truncates** the file, so a failure halfway leaves it partially written.
- `os.Create` or `os.OpenFile` give you an `*os.File`, an `io.Writer`. Wrap it in a
  `bufio.Writer` when you make many small writes, and call `Flush` at the end.
- To replace a file that something else depends on, write a temp file in the same
  directory, `Sync` and `Close` it, then `os.Rename` it over the target. Until the rename,
  readers see the complete old file; after it, the complete new one.

The `perm` argument (`0o644`, `0o600`) is only used when the file is **created**, and the
process umask is subtracted from it on Unix (a umask of `022` turns `0o666` into `0o644`).
On Windows only the owner-write bit means anything: without it the file gets the
read-only attribute. That's why the examples never print modes: they would differ by OS.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C: `os.OpenFile` flags are `open(2)`'s (`O_APPEND`, `O_CREATE`, `O_EXCL`, `O_TRUNC`),
  and `bufio.Writer` is the buffering `stdio` does for `FILE*`, made explicit. As with
  `fclose`, the close can be where a write error shows up.
- Java: no atomic write either. The idiom is `Files.createTempFile(dir, ...)`, write, then
  `Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE)`; Go's `os.Rename` is that move. Java's checked
  `IOException` on `close()` forces you to think about a failed close; in Go only you (and
  linters such as `errcheck`) notice a dropped `Close` error.
- Python: `os.replace(tmp, target)` is the same rename, and `tempfile.mkstemp(dir=...)`
  is `os.CreateTemp(dir, pattern)`, mode `0o600` included.
- Node: `fs.writeFileSync` truncates and writes like `os.WriteFile`; there's no built-in
  atomic write there either (npm packages such as `write-file-atomic` do this dance).

## How it works

`writeAtomic` in the second example, step by step:

1. `os.CreateTemp(dir, "atomic.json.tmp-*")` creates a new file with a random name and
   mode `0o600`. Several processes can do this at once without colliding.
2. Write the content. Nobody reads this name, so a crash here only leaves a stray temp file.
3. `f.Chmod(perm)`, then `f.Sync()` so the bytes are on stable storage, then `f.Close()`.
4. `os.Rename(tmp, target)` swaps the name. On Linux and macOS, `rename(2)` within one file
   system is atomic: other processes see the old file or the new one, never a mix.

Go's own docs for `os.Rename` add a caveat: "Even within the same directory, on non-Unix
platforms Rename is not an atomic operation." On Windows the pattern still guarantees the
target is never a half-written file, because the new content is complete before it gets
the name; just don't rely on readers never seeing a gap. Replacing a file that another
Windows process holds open (an editor, an antivirus scan) can also fail, so retry or report.

## Design notes

Accept an `io.Writer` (or a `func(io.Writer) error`, as `writeAtomic` does) in code that
produces content, and decide at the edge whether it goes to a file, a buffer in a test, or an
HTTP response. Reserve the atomic dance for files that are read while you write or must
survive a crash; for an export the user downloads once, `bufio` plus a checked `Close` is
enough. On Linux, a rename is durable only after the parent directory is synced too
(`fsync` on the directory), which databases do and most applications skip; PostgreSQL's
write-ahead log is the industrial version of the same idea.

before Flush: 4096 bytes in the file, 2583 in the buffer
after Flush and Close: 6679 bytes

O_EXCL on an existing file is fs.ErrExist: true

in place: simulated crash
atomic:   simulated crash
inplace.json valid JSON: false {"version":2,"ci
atomic.json  valid JSON: true  {"version":1,"city":"İzmir"}
